summary: Updates RFC 4944 with a protocol for forwarding individual fragments across a route-over mesh and recovering lost ones end to end, with congestion control to protect the network. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: If one piece of a cut-up message gets lost in a mesh of small devices, this lets the sender resend just that piece, and not the whole message, without causing a traffic jam.

questions: what is an rfrag ack bitmap
subtitle: Forwards pieces of a big packet across a low-power mesh and resends only the pieces that went missing.

tldr.problem: The original 6LoWPAN fragmentation in RFC 4944 needs the packet to be reassembled at every hop of a route-over mesh, has no selective recovery (one lost fragment fails the whole datagram), no congestion control and no way to abort.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8931 adds two dispatch types: RFRAG carries a fragment that intermediate routers forward by label along a path set up by the first fragment, and RFRAG-ACK returns a 32-bit bitmap that tells the sender exactly which fragments arrived. An ECN flag and an acknowledgment-request flag give basic congestion control.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4944. Deployments are expected to be managed and homogeneous, and the RFC says an incremental transition requires a flag day.

today: RFC 8931 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4944 and builds on the generic fragment-forwarding behavior of RFC 8930. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Problem with Fragments in a Mesh
sections.content:
Most low-power and lossy network (LLN) traffic is tiny, and an IEEE 802.15.4 frame can carry a payload of 74 bytes or more, so fragmentation is usually not needed. It is still required for mission-critical jobs such as firmware upgrades or pulling logs, where the data can be on the order of 10 KB or more and needs reliable end-to-end transport.

The original 6LoWPAN fragmentation in RFC 4944 has several weaknesses:

  • Routing across a route-over mesh requires reassembly at each hop, which adds latency and uses scarce memory and battery.
  • There is no selective recovery: if one fragment is not delivered, the whole datagram fails, and the reassembling endpoint holds buffers until a timeout.
  • A loss at an intermediate hop is not noticed by either endpoint, so the source keeps sending and wastes resources.
  • There is no congestion control and no way to abort a multi-fragment transmission from either end.

This RFC forwards fragments over typically a few hops and adds a selective acknowledgment between the endpoints. Flow control is out of scope because the endpoints are expected to be able to store the full datagram.
sections.eli5: Little devices have tiny mailboxes. Before, every station had to rebuild the whole letter, and one lost card ruined everything. This design fixes both problems.

sections.title: How It Builds on RFC 8930
sections.content:
The generic technique, 6LoWPAN Fragment Forwarding (6LFF), is specified in RFC 8930, and this RFC is one concrete instance of it. Routing information is fully in the first fragment, which is forwarded first. Each router builds a Virtual Reassembly Buffer (VRB) state from it and uses that to forward the next fragments along the same path, much like MPLS label switching. The Datagram_Tag acts as the label and is swapped at each hop.

This RFC extends RFC 8930 in four ways:

  • No slack for refragmenting: intermediate nodes cannot refragment, because fragments are recovered end to end by sequence number. The first fragment MUST leave enough slack for less efficient compression at later hops, for example an assumed MTU that is 8 bytes smaller when the source IID is elided.
  • Inter-frame gap: a configurable gap between frames to the same next hop protects against hidden-terminal collisions on a single-frequency mesh.
  • Congestion control: fragments are grouped in windows with intermediate acknowledgments, and an ECN mechanism can adapt window size, fragment size or the gap. The mechanism for tuning those is out of scope.
  • Modifying the first fragment: if compression of the hop limit, addresses or Routing Header changes en route, the intermediate node MUST adapt the Datagram_Size and add the saved difference to the Fragment_Offset of later fragments.

Headers that cannot fit in the first fragment MUST NOT be compressed, consistent with RFC 6282.
sections.eli5: The first card carries the full address, and each station remembers where to pass the rest, like a line of dominoes. Stations also leave small pauses between cards so they do not bump into each other.

sections.title: The RFRAG Fragment Header
sections.content:
The RFRAG header starts with the dispatch pattern 1110100, followed by these fields:

  • E (1 bit): ECN. The source clears it and intermediate routers set it to signal congestion.
  • Datagram_Tag (8 bits): an identifier of the datagram, locally unique to the link-layer sender.
  • X (1 bit): Ack-Request. When set, the fragmenting endpoint requires an acknowledgment.
  • Sequence (5 bits): the fragment number, from 0 to at most 31. Sequence 0 marks the first fragment.
  • Fragment_Size (10 bits): size of this fragment, in bytes unless a link layer says otherwise, allowing up to 1023 bytes.
  • Fragment_Offset (16 bits): in the first fragment it carries the Datagram_Size of the compressed packet. In others it is the offset in the compressed datagram.

Sizes and offsets refer to the compressed form of the packet. The Sequence is not tied to position, which lets a lost fragment be split into smaller ones with new sequence numbers when the MTU turns out to be smaller. A Fragment_Offset of 0 signals an abort, and the state for the datagram is cleaned up. The last fragment is recognized when its offset plus size equals the stored Datagram_Size.
sections.eli5: Each postcard says which letter it belongs to, which number it is, how big it is, where it goes, and whether the sender wants a reply right now.

sections.title: The Acknowledgment and Its Bitmap
sections.content:
The RFRAG Acknowledgment (RFRAG-ACK) uses the dispatch pattern 1110101, an E flag that echoes ECN, an 8-bit Datagram_Tag that is locally unique to the link-layer recipient, and a 32-bit RFRAG Acknowledgment Bitmap.

Bit x of the bitmap is set when the fragment with Sequence x was received. The RFC's example shows fragments 0 to 20 received except for 1, 2 and 16, which must be retried. Two special values matter. A NULL bitmap (all zeros) means the fragmentation process is aborted. A FULL bitmap (all ones) means the datagram was completely received, whichever fragments were used to cover it. This is how intermediate nodes learn unambiguously that the transfer is complete, even when a fragment was retried as several smaller ones.
sections.eli5: The receiver sends back a checklist with 32 boxes. A tick means that card arrived. A blank list means stop, and a fully ticked list means all done.

sections.title: Forwarding and Recovering Fragments
sections.content:
On the first fragment, an intermediate router creates a VRB with LSP state indexed by the incoming interface, previous-hop link-layer address and Datagram_Tag. It forwards the fragment by the IPv6 route, swaps the tag, and also keeps reverse state so an RFRAG-ACK can flow back. The IPv6 header MUST be in the first fragment in full. Later fragments follow the same path and cannot take an alternate route. If a later fragment arrives with no matching VRB, the router answers with an RFRAG-ACK carrying a NULL bitmap.

Windows and retries. The Ack-Request flag marks the end of a window. It MUST be set on the last fragment if the sender wants automatic repeat request (ARQ), and MAY be set on earlier fragments for congestion control. A receiver MUST answer a fragment that has it set. The ARQ process MUST be protected by a Retransmission Timeout (RTO) timer, with exponential backoff. Fragments MUST be sent round-robin: all fragments first, then lost ones oldest first.

Completion and aborts. When the whole datagram is in, the receiver sends a FULL bitmap and runs a short timer to absorb stragglers. An abort is signaled forward with a pseudo fragment whose Fragment_Offset is 0, or backward with a NULL bitmap, and receiving a NULL bitmap makes the sender stop, except that it MAY retry the first fragment through another next hop. The RFC also describes using the scheme along a diverse path, a 6TiSCH Track.
sections.eli5: The sender sends all the cards, then resends the missing ones in order. Whenever someone says stop, every station on the path throws away what it remembered about that letter.

sections.title: Management Parameters
sections.content:
The management system SHOULD supply parameters, and an implementation MUST stay inside the configured limits. The new settings only apply to the fragmenting endpoint, because echoing ECN is always on.

  • Inter-frame gap: minimum time between transmissions. It MUST at least protect one transmission from colliding with the next, and SHOULD be increased as needed to protect the network.
  • Fragment sizes: MinFragmentSize, OptFragmentSize and MaxFragmentSize. The maximum MUST be less than 512 if the PHY unit is the byte.
  • Window_Size: MUST be at least 1 and less than 33. A value of 32, meaning only the last fragment is acknowledged, is RECOMMENDED in half-duplex LLNs. A small value of 3 SHOULD be used in full-duplex networks.
  • ARQ timeouts: MinARQTimeOut, OptARQTimeOut (3 times the maximum expected round-trip time RECOMMENDED) and MaxARQTimeOut.
  • Retries: MaxFragRetries, default of 3 RECOMMENDED, and MaxDatagramRetries, default of 1 RECOMMENDED.
  • UseECN: whether the sender reacts to congestion signals.

Operators should monitor retries and ECN settings and tune the optimum fragment and window sizes for the next datagrams.
sections.eli5: There are dials for how big each card is, how many to send before waiting, how long to wait and how many times to try again. The RFC suggests starting values for some of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This RFC inherits the security considerations of RFC 8930. It adds that an on-path attacker can end a transmission early by sending a forged RFRAG Acknowledgment. It can also cause extra transmissions by clearing bits in the bitmap, and extra acknowledgments by forcing the Ack-Request bit on fragments it forwards.

The fragmentation protocol has no native security, so secure joining and link-layer security are REQUIRED. An attacker on the path can also slow or discard packets, which reduces throughput. The 8-bit Datagram_Tag wraps sooner than in RFC 4944, but the RFC judges 256 values to be plenty for constrained nodes that hold only one or a few large packets. The VRB state could be used for denial of service, but this scheme keeps no data in that state that would not fit in the previous fragment.
sections.eli5: Anyone standing on the path could lie in the checklist and make the sender stop or resend things. The only protection is locking the network itself, since the messages have no locks of their own.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: ECN, set by routers on congestion.

fields.name: Datagram_Tag
fields.desc: Datagram label, locally unique to the sender.

fields.name: Sequence
fields.desc: Fragment number; 0 marks the first fragment.

fields.name: Fragment_Offset
fields.desc: Datagram_Size in the first fragment, otherwise the offset; 0 means abort.

fields.name: Datagram_Tag
fields.desc: Datagram label, locally unique to the recipient.

fields.name: RFRAG Acknowledgment Bitmap
fields.desc: Bit x set means Sequence x was received. All zeros aborts, all ones completes.
